overview.body: Welcome to Bat City Collective! You've just joined Austin's hottest indie game studio as a junior developer. Your first project? Building a Texas road trip game for our client, All My Eggses Live in Texas. In this lab you'll build the travel calculator: get the player's name, take a dice roll, and work out how far that roll gets you toward each destination.

mentorQuote.quote: Hey, welcome aboard! Here's the habit that'll save you more time than anything else this semester: write a few lines, run them, check them, then write a few more. Every checkpoint on this sheet ends with a run and a submit. Don't skip them. The lab sheet is the spec. The videos show you the thinking, and the book is your reference, but if they ever disagree, the sheet wins.

objectives: Get a roll from 1 to 20 and turn it into a whole number with int()
Turn the roll into miles with a named constant
Calculate the miles left to each of 4 destinations
Display a Travel Report, and test it with more than one roll
overview.textbookReference: Starting Out with Python, 6th Edition by Tony Gaddis, Chapter 2: Input, Processing, and Output

namedConstants.description: Miles one point on the roll is worth (10)

namedConstants.description: San Antonio to Corpus Christi (150 miles)

Your program MUST define the 5 named constants and use them in the calculations

Your program MUST calculate the miles left to all 4 destinations

timeGuide.strategy: CodeGrade checks the checkpoints in order, and it starts on the next one only when the current one passes. The percentages are each checkpoint's share of the output tests; style and documentation are scored on the whole file. Run your program after every few lines, and submit at the end of every checkpoint. When something fails, fix one thing, run it, and resubmit.

content.body: The file every lab in this course starts from: a header at the top, the named constants, the main() structure, and the game's banner. At the end of this checkpoint your program runs and prints the banner.

CodeGrade reads your header for your name, ID, and section, and it scores the header and your docstrings on every lab. Those points are free once the format is right, so get it right once here and copy it forward. Named constants keep the game's numbers in one place: if a distance changes, you change one line.

items: Open your lab-1-1 folder in VS Code (it's in the course starter download) and open the empty lab-1-1.py inside it. If you make the file yourself, the name must be exactly lab-1-1.py: lowercase L, hyphens, the digit one.

At the very top of the file, type this header. Put in your own name, abc123, and section (908, ON1, or ON2). Keep the labels exactly as shown, each with its colon, and keep the closing """ on a line by itself. Write the Description in your own words.

content.title: Where every line you add goes
content.body_html:
def main(): gives your program a name, and the main() line at the bottom runs it. From here on, every line you add goes inside main(): indented four spaces, below the banner, and above the two empty lines before if __name__.

  • Type def main(): only once. A second one causes the "redefinition of unused 'main'" style error.
  • The if __name__ == '__main__': line stays at the very bottom, at the left margin, with main() indented under it.
  • Each block of code starts with a # comment line saying what it does, with one empty line above it. Type the comments shown in the steps: CodeGrade's Documentation check looks for at least three.
  • Empty lines must be truly empty. A space or tab on an empty line is a style error.

content.body: The game's first conversation: it asks the player's name and greets them by name.

input() shows a prompt, waits for the player to type, and hands back what they typed as text. An f-string drops a variable's value into a message. Those two together are how every game in this course talks to the player.

content.body: The dice roll. The player types a number from 1 to 20, the game turns it into miles, and it shows where you can go from San Antonio.

Everything input() hands back is text, even when the player types a number. int() turns that text into a whole number you can do math with. This pattern, input then convert then use, is the most common shape in Python programs. You'll write it constantly in this course.

content.body: The math: how many miles are left to each destination after your roll, including Galveston, which you reach through Houston. Then the Travel Report that shows it all.

Each calculation gets its own line and its own variable, so you can check each one by itself. Galveston takes two steps: first the total distance, then what's left after your roll. And one run can't prove your math: a mistake can look right on one roll and wrong on another. That's why you'll test three rolls.

items: Leave one empty line after the destination list, then calculate the miles left to each destination. Every line is distance first, then minus miles_rolled:

content.code:
# Miles left to each destination
    corpus_remaining = SAT_TO_CORPUS - miles_rolled
    houston_remaining = SAT_TO_HOUSTON - miles_rolled
    austin_remaining = SAT_TO_AUSTIN - miles_rolled
    galveston_total = SAT_TO_HOUSTON + HOU_TO_GALVESTON
    galveston_remaining = galveston_total - miles_rolled

content.body: VS Code underlines these new names as unused for now. The underlines go away in the next step, when the report prints them.

items: Leave one empty line, then print the Travel Report:

content.code:
# Travel report
    print('=' * 50)
    print('TRAVEL REPORT')
    print('=' * 50)
    print(f'Driver: {player_name}')
    print('Miles remaining after your roll:')
    print(f'  Corpus Christi: {corpus_remaining}')
    print(f'  Houston: {houston_remaining}')
    print(f'  Austin: {austin_remaining}')
    print(f'  Galveston (via Houston): {galveston_remaining}')
    print()
    print('Zero or less = you made it!')
    print('More than zero = you still have miles to go.')
    print()

rows: A number has the wrong sign: 50 where the sheet shows -50, or the other way around

That subtraction is backwards. It's distance first, then minus miles_rolled: SAT_TO_CORPUS - miles_rolled. A backwards Corpus Christi line still shows 0 on roll 15, because 150 minus 150 is 0 either way. That's why one roll isn't enough.
Galveston is wrong
Check both steps: galveston_total adds the two distances, then galveston_remaining subtracts miles_rolled from that total.
Style error E501: line too long
Do the math on its own line and print the variable, the way the steps above do. Don't put the calculation inside the f-string.
NameError on a constant
The name doesn't match the constant at the top of your file. Check the spelling and the capital letters.

ifSomethingBreaks.symptom: Output shows {player_name} or {roll} instead of a value
ifSomethingBreaks.redirect: Check the line that prints it: the f before the opening quote is missing.

ifSomethingBreaks.symptom: A report number has the wrong sign (50 instead of -50, or the other way around)
ifSomethingBreaks.redirect: Check CP4 (Travel Report): that subtraction is backwards. Distance first, then minus miles_rolled. Run rolls 1 and 20 too; roll 15 can hide it.

ifYouGetStuck: Re-read the checkpoint you're on, and run the program again with that checkpoint's inputs
Submit to CodeGrade and read the first problem it names. Fix that one, then resubmit
Check the BookEx reference: the patterns are there
